summary: Describes a packet explosion problem that can happen with mutual encapsulation of protocols, where protocol A encapsulates B and B also encapsulates A. It is an informational warning about this design mistake.

eli5.summary: If you put a letter in an envelope and that envelope in another that goes back into the first kind, the pile grows forever. This paper warns about that.

subtitle: How nested protocol wrapping can cause runaway packet growth.

tldr.problem: When two protocols can encapsulate each other (A wraps B and B wraps A), a routing loop causes packets to grow exponentially as they gain layers of headers.
tldr.mechanism: Without hop count preservation across encapsulation layers, packets that loop grow with each encapsulation, eventually fragmenting and creating an exponential packet explosion.
tldr.outcome: The RFC warns against mutual encapsulation and recommends preserving hop counts, filtering repeated headers, or avoiding the pattern entirely.

facts.label: MTU problem
facts.value: Fragments continue looping, causing exponential growth

today: RFC 1326 remains a design warning applicable to modern protocols. While classic mutual encapsulation scenarios are rare in production networks, the lesson guides protocol design decisions. Tunneling, overlay networks, and virtualization layers now dominant in networking benefit from these warnings about uncontrolled layering.

sections.title: The Mutual Encapsulation Problem
sections.content: As different network protocols multiplied, systems often needed to interwork. One approach is encapsulation: wrapping one protocol inside another. But sometimes this becomes mutual: protocol A runs over protocol B in some cases, and protocol B runs over protocol A in other cases. Examples include both IP over AppleTalk and AppleTalk over IP. This flexibility creates a hidden danger.
sections.eli5: Different mail systems need to talk to each other, so sometimes one wraps letters meant for the other. But what if both wrapping systems can wrap each other?

sections.title: How Packet Explosion Happens
sections.content: Consider a network where a backbone uses protocol X, another uses protocol Y, and four stub networks split between them. When a router needs to send a packet across a backbone using a different protocol, it encapsulates the packet. If a routing loop forms so that packets bounce between the two backbones, the result is catastrophic. A packet from left S(X) reaches a router Rc, which wraps it in Y to cross B(Y). Router Rb then wraps the Y-wrapped packet in X to cross B(X). The packet now has headers X<Y<X>. Each encapsulation adds another layer. The packet grows exponentially: Y<X<Y<X>>, then X<Y<X<Y<X>>>, and so on. Once the packet reaches the Maximum Transmission Unit (MTU) size, it fragments. Each fragment continues looping and growing, creating an exponential explosion of packets.
sections.eli5: A message bounces between two routes, and each route wraps it again in its own envelope. Soon the package is larger than a truck.

sections.title: Why This Happens and Why It Is Hard to Fix
sections.content: The explosion persists until links are saturated. If looping packets drown out routing updates and management packets, the loop may not break itself automatically and requires manual intervention. Several potential fixes exist, but each has pitfalls. Preserving hop count information would help, but not all protocols have hop counts, and ranges differ (AppleTalk max 16 hops, IP up to 256). Routers could peek into headers to detect repeated encapsulation, but they may not recognize all protocols or may be encrypting packets. Nested mutual encapsulation scenarios legitimately require multiple instances of the same header, making blind filtering incorrect.
sections.eli5: Fixing this is tricky because some letters may legitimately need multiple wrappers, and routers might not even understand all the wrapping types.

sections.title: Recommendations
sections.content: The RFC recommends a hybrid approach: outlaw nested mutual encapsulation where possible, employ both hop count preservation and header peeking where appropriate, and generally discourage mutual encapsulation. Those who engage in mutual encapsulation must be aware of the risk and accept the consequences. The fundamental lesson is that protocol designers should avoid creating situations where A encapsulates B and B also encapsulates A.
sections.eli5: The best solution is to avoid putting two protocols in a situation where they can wrap each other. If you must, be very careful.

references.text: Shoch, J., Cohen, D., and D. Taft, "Mutual Encapsulation of Internetwork Protocols", Computer Networks 5, North-Holland, 1981, 287-300.
